Known Variance Sample Size for a Fixed Width Interval for a Normal Mean

Source: R/seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal.R
seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal.Rd

Returns the sample size at which a confidence interval for the mean of a normal distribution has half width d when the population variance is known. This is the benchmark that the purely sequential (seq_fwd_norm_mean) and two stage (ts_fwd_norm_mean) fixed width procedures aim for without knowing the variance. It is useful for planning with an assumed variance and for judging how much a sequential procedure costs relative to knowing the variance in advance.

Usage

seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal(variance, d, conf_level = 0.95)

Arguments

variance

The population variance \(\sigma^2\) (the square of the standard deviation, not the standard deviation itself). A single positive number, in the squared units of the data.

d

The half width of the confidence interval (the margin of error), in the units of the data. A single positive number. The full width is \(2d\).

conf_level

The confidence level, strictly between 0 and 1. Default 0.95.

Value

A length one integer of at least 1: the smallest sample size \(n\) for which the known variance interval \(\bar{X}_n \pm d\) has confidence level at least conf_level, that is, \(\lceil C \rceil\).

Details

With known variance \(\sigma^2\) the interval \(\bar{X}_n \pm d\) covers the mean with probability \(2\Phi(d \sqrt{n} / \sigma) - 1\), which reaches the confidence level \(1 - \alpha\) when \(n\) is at least $$C = \frac{z_{\alpha/2}^2 \, \sigma^2}{d^2},$$ where \(z_{\alpha/2}\) is the upper \(\alpha/2\) point of the standard normal distribution. \(C\) is rarely a whole number; the function returns the smallest whole sample size at which the coverage is at least the confidence level, which is \(C\) rounded up and never less than 1. (When \(C\) is within rounding error of a whole number, the coverage formula decides between that number and the next.) The unrounded value is qnorm((1 - conf_level) / 2, lower.tail = FALSE)^2 * variance / d^2.

Because the result is proportional to the variance, a planning value that is too small gives a sample that is too small by the same factor. When the variance is not known, use one of the procedures that estimate it as the data arrive.

References

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

seq_fwd_norm_mean and ts_fwd_norm_mean, which reach the same target without knowing the variance; seq_budget_optimal for the corresponding known parameter allocation in the budget constrained procedure.

Other seq_fwd_norm_mean: seq_fwd_norm_mean(), seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Francis Bilson Darku fbilsond@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Mean score on a 100 point skills assessment to within 2 points, with
# 95% confidence, if the standard deviation were known to be 8.
seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal(variance = 8^2, d = 2)
#> [1] 62

# The same target at 99% confidence.
seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal(variance = 8^2, d = 2, conf_level = 0.99)
#> [1] 107
